summary.text: A 49-year-old woman presented to a local hospital with a week of progressive yellowing of the skin and sclera, yellowish urine, lighter stool, itching and fatigue. She had repeatedly used traditional Chinese medicinal remedies in the year before onset and denied a family history of genetic diseases. Examination showed marked jaundice with no ascites, hepatosplenomegaly or encephalopathy signs, and initial tests showed elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin and hypercholesterolemia.

Autoimmune, viral hepatitis and tumor markers were negative, and genetic testing excluded familial hypercholesterolemia and urea cycle disorders. MRCP and contrast CT in November 2023 showed common hepatic duct stenosis, mild biliary obstruction, thickened common bile duct walls, suspicious duodenal nodules, cholecystitis and diffuse liver lesions without cirrhosis. She was diagnosed with drug-cholestatic hepatitis using the Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method, and liver biopsy on January 31, 2024 confirmed drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis.

Liver-protecting drugs at the local hospital did not prevent deterioration, so intravenous methylprednisolone was started on December 6, 2023 and improved bilirubin and appetite, but liver function rebounded on tapering and high-dose methylprednisolone was continued. She was transferred on January 1, 2024 and switched to oral methylprednisolone, which was reduced and stopped on January 22. Severe hyperlipidemia (total cholesterol 50.59 mmol/L) was unresponsive to fenofibrate, ezetimibe or a strict vegan diet.

She was discharged on March 1 on regular liver-protecting medications with liver function improving steadily. As of July 26 GGT and ALP remained elevated, total cholesterol had fallen to 6.28 mmol/L and triglycerides were normal on UDCA and statin therapy. At the most recent review on December 29 total cholesterol was 6.47 mmol/L, GGT 197.2 U/L and ALP 192.9 U/L, with other liver function within normal parameters.

caption_evidence.quote: Changes of biochemistry parameters during hospitalization.

figures.caption_summary:
Figure 1
Changes of biochemistry parameters during hospitalization. The patient had worsening liver function over the first 7 days after receiving common liver-protecting medications, then the glucocorticosteroid therapy was performed, resulting in a significant improvement. Although we had gradually tapered the hormones due to the fact that her serum bilirubin was plateauing and lipid levels were too high, we still observed that those levels were slowly trending down after the glucocorticosteroid therapy was completely stopped. AST: Aspartate aminotransferase; DBIL: Direct bilirubin; ALB: Albumin; GGT: Gamma-glutamyl transferase; ALP: Alkaline phosphatase; ALT: Alanine aminotransferase; TBIL: Total bilirubin.

figures.caption_summary:
Figure 3
Histological findings of an ultrasound-guided percutaneous liver biopsy stained with hematoxylin and eosin (magnification × 10). A histological examination revealed severe lobular hepatitis, accompanied by bile duct injury and intrahepatic cholestasis, and a loss of bile duct structure around portal tracts with a small amount of visible lymphocytes and plasma cell infiltration, which was believed to be the result of drug-related liver injury.

article_limitations: Caption-layer visual status not_inspected; the three JPEGs were inspected in the separate visual target.
Table 1 HDL-C and LDL-C cells for November 25, 2023 are dashes and are not recorded as values; the figure-embedded data table prints 0 for those cells, which is not treated as a result.

Arrow-listed serial values in the Laboratory examinations text carry no dates; they are recorded undated and are not mapped to Table 1 dates or to each other, except lipid values the text explicitly cites to Table 1.
Values printed on the plotted biochemistry chart (Figure 1) were not transcribed as facts.

Blood ammonia is described as normal (laboratory section and follow-up) and as consistently high (Discussion); all three statements are review-only (laboratory-section normal and Discussion high as source_conflict, follow-up normal as ambiguous).
The abdomen is described as non-tender and as having mild right upper quadrant tenderness in the same examination paragraph; kept as review-only source conflict.
Discussion mechanisms, literature statements, pseudohyponatremia, Lp-X and general recommendations are not patient facts; the patient-specific chylous plasma statement is recorded.
Year is not stated for July 26, December 29, March 1 and January 22 events; no ISO dates assigned.
Statin, fenofibrate and ezetimibe use is stated only as ineffective, unresponsive or maintained, without doses or start and stop dates.

Parent decision: the trailing (local hospital, November 2023) in b00026 closes only the no-cirrhosis sentence, so the first-sentence findings and the MRCP/CT procedure items carry no time; the single-sentence b00027/b00028/b00030-b00033 parentheticals govern their own sentences.

Figure 1 has no date axis and the left-to-right order of its printed values is opposite to its glucocorticosteroid arrows; Figure 2 plots values in the order opposite to its own data table; no chronology is taken from either image.

Undated arrow values in b00017/b00018 duplicate numerically identical dated or labelled values elsewhere (initial labs, discharge review, follow-up); they are not merged by number matching, so some measurements may appear twice.
